title: Backtesting tool is built to test your own trading strategies — properly, with real statistical rigor (looking for testers)
author: DeliciousEquipment13
selftext:
Hi all — I built a tool called Mithos, and I'm looking for a few people to use the strategy-building and backtesting side of it.



What it actually is: you build your own trading strategy from a library of components (breakouts, trailing stops, filters, etc.), and it runs through a genuinely rigorous statistical validation process before telling you honestly whether it holds up — walk-forward testing across held-back windows, a placebo control (checking your result beats random entries, not just looks good), a penalty that gets stricter the more variations you've tried, and a real cost floor so a backtest doesn't quietly ignore spread/commission.



What it isn't: a signal service, an "AI trading bot," or anything promising guaranteed returns. It doesn't tell you what to trade. On my own test account, 18 of the last 20 strategy ideas I ran through it were correctly rejected — including some I genuinely thought looked promising going in. That's the tool working as intended, not a sales pitch gone wrong.



This is specifically the backtesting/strategy-builder side. Build an idea, see if it survives real scrutiny, nothing else required.



Why I'm posting: I want people who aren't me actually building strategies, trying to break things, and telling me honestly where it's confusing or wrong. Any ideas for additional building blocks are WELCOME!



[www.mithos.co.uk](http://www.mithos.co.uk)

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
The validation stack you describe (walk-forward, placebo entries, multiple-testing penalty, cost floor) is the right one, and a 18-of-20 rejection rate is a good sign the tool is honest.

Building block idea: **event-aware components**. For example, an "earnings/macro blackout" filter (skip entries within N hours of a scheduled release), a "post-event drift" entry (trade only after a defined reaction window), and an "event-day flag" so results can be split into event vs. non-event trades. Many strategies that pass validation are quietly earning their edge from event days, and a placebo test can't tell you that unless the events are tagged. It also helps with cost realism, since spreads widen around releases.

The catch is the calendar has to be point-in-time, with exact release timestamps and correct time zones, or the filter itself introduces look-ahead. That's the layer we build at Cymetica with EventTrader, structured, timestamped events you could plug in as a data source for those components.
